name: Ivory-Caldera
description: Ivory-Caldera is a pale furnace: its supervolcanoes erupt ash so fine and mineral-white that the whole surface reads as bone from orbit, cracked in black basalt where fresh lava has drawn new seams. Four calderas the size of seas vent in slow rotation, each in turn filling the sky with columns that can be seen from neighboring systems. Between eruptions the plains glow dull cherry at every fissure.

The toxic atmosphere carries acid rain that falls warm and hisses when it strikes stone; the air tastes of metal through any filter, and sound is a constant low roar punctuated by the deep percussion of distant collapse. At night—what passes for night—the lava fields throw light upward onto clouds until the whole sky glows like a forge seen through smoke.

Nothing here is artificial, which is precisely what unsettles survey teams: the volcanic cycle runs on a schedule too regular by half, each caldera erupting within hours of prediction across three centuries of observation. Geologists have stopped publishing the model's constants, because the constants keep converging—toward a date roughly two hundred years out.

The uranium lodes are extraordinary, the geothermal potential effectively infinite, and extraction remains theoretical: unshielded rigs last days in the acid rain, and shielded ones cost more than they yield. Two consortiums are quietly developing acid-proof automation anyway. The planet, meanwhile, keeps perfect time.
